premises.text: Online fashion lacks personalization of fit, so most fashion still sells in stores on standard models unlike real people
premises.evidence_span: What's missing in online fashion shopping is personalization. People still don't know how clothes fit when they're buying online

premises.text: Shoppers create a true-to-size 3D personal model from two fit questions and try on outfits in-browser without special hardware
premises.evidence_span: create your own model and try on clothes on that model

premises.text: Designers' collections are digitized at scale and offered to retailers via API with pay-as-you-go pricing and no upfront cost
premises.evidence_span: we offer this collection to the retailers who carry these designers using our API

premises.text: Retailers get analytics on consumer sizes and popular styles to optimize operations
premises.evidence_span: They get access to all the sizes from the consumers. They also get access for the popular styles and the sizes from their clothes

value.text: Shoppers see how clothes truly fit online so more fashion commerce moves online
value.evidence_span: a new way to shop online

secondary_value.text: Retailers increase sales and reduce returns
secondary_value.evidence_span: They get increased sales, reduced returns

causal_links.evidence_span: People still don't know how clothes fit when they're buying online
retailers have no upfront costs. They pay us as they go

notes: 90% in-store and model-mismatch folded into fit-personalization problem (§4.1.6). Drag-drop, zoom, rotate, side-by-side sizes, and outfit styling folded into true-to-size fitting cascade (§4.1.7). Facebook share as feature of that surface. Mass-customization/digitize-before-manufacture treated as vision framing for platform, not extra premise (§4.1.4). Designer logos as traction. Anti-template: problem, fitting UX, and retailer API economics separately revisable.
